utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. For the record, we have got two accused missing. The first one is Accused Borovcanin. The information that the Trial Chamber has is that he had a dental appointment and should be able to join us in the course of the sitting later on this morning, but I still need a confirmation from his Defence team that there is no objection for the Trial Chamber to proceed with the trial; in other words, that he's waived his right to be present for the part for which he will be absent. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The information that I have is exactly the same as the Trial Chamber. The information is that Mr. Borovcanin had a scheduled a -- one small dentist intervention, and he will join us later during the course of the trial. He waived his right for being present at least for a part of today's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, please, we will still require the waiver in writing, and you will attend to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honour, I will provide the Trial Chamber with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure you will, Mr. Lazarevic. The other absentee is General Pandurevic. You will recall that we had granted a special provisional release from custody, and he was to supposed to return here by not later than the 8th of January. Unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is some interference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Due to unforeseen circumstances, which were beyond the control of General Pandurevic and others, he couldn't travel from Sarajevo on the day he was scheduled to travel because of the weather conditions there, the fog. We've tried to make alternative arrangements, but they were not successful. He will be arriving, hopefully, later on today in the afternoon. I understand, at least from the information we have received, that he also would waive his right to be present for today's sitting and that the formal communication is going to be confirmed by Mr. Haynes. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, it is. He spoke to Mr. Sarapa yesterday indicated that he was happy for proceedings to proceed in his absence, and a signed confirmation of that will be with the Trial Chamber today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Otherwise, the other accused are present. As far as representation is concerned, I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic and of Mr. Sarapa. I don't see Mr. Sarapa, but I am not sure. No Mr. Sarapa. For the Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer, and I think we can begin. First of all, I would like to welcome you all back. I also appreciate the efforts you made, Mr. Zivanovic, because you also had problems in trying to return in time, and that you have succeeded in finding a solution, because otherwise we would have really had a compounded problem. So I appreciate that. General Miletic, our condolences for the demise of your sister. We would have granted a variation of the provisional release conditions had the Government of Republika Srpska provided the necessary guarantees in time, but that, I understand, was not possible. There are some preliminaries -- THE ACCUSED MILETIC: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are some preliminaries. There is a Prosecution motion filed recently on the 8th of January, requesting an order admitting a representative of the United States government to be present in Court during the testimony of Richard Butler, who as you know is due to start his testimony probably tomorrow, at the latest Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any objection from any of the Defence teams? Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, there isn't. Indeed, we had the opportunity, when everybody had finally made it back from Belgrade yesterday, to discuss it yesterday evening, and we're of the view that if there is to be any objection to questioning of Mr. Butler about his antecedental career, then the American government is appropriate authority to make such objection rather anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for your statement and position, which I understand is taken on behalf of all the Defence teams, and so your motion, Mr. McCloskey, is hereby being orally granted. It will not be followed by a written decision, so you only need to communicate the oral decision to the Embassy of the United States here in The Hague. There is also, a few days after we started the recess, the Prosecution filed a motion for leave to amend its 65 ter exhibit list with exhibits pertaining to Witness Richard Butler. This was filed confidentially on the 18th of December, 2007. I don't need to go into the merits or the details as regards these documents. What I would like to know is whether any of the Defence teams are opposing this motion or not. Ordinarily, you would have been expected to file a response by the 2nd of January. That was the moratorium that we had granted on the 14th of December, when we last sat, which would presumably apply to this motion as well. But now we are all back, the session started on the 7th of January, even though we are sitting for the first time today. Mr. Butler is due to testify either tomorrow, or at the latest Monday, so we need to know what your position is, because we need to decide this. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Subject to the opportunity of speaking to Mr. McCloskey perhaps at the first break, this motion is likely to receive opposition, I can inform you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we'll postpone this until after the first break, and please keep in mind that due to the proximity or to the urgency of the matter, we now need to decide it. I don't think there is anything else that we need to raise for the time being, unless you have preliminaries yourselves. I recognise Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't want to prompt any unnecessary preliminaries, but the other matter that we did discuss, about which I'm authorised and able to give you an immediate response, is the Prosecution's motion of the 2nd of January relating to the 18 additional witnesses and the application that they be received under Rule 92 bis. But that can perhaps wait until Mr. Kingori has finished his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, we filed the motion. We haven't had any discussions with our friends with respect to the motion, so we would be prepared to orally argue the issue at a -- after a break or towards the end of the day, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any further preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we can safely bring in Mr. Kingori. My understanding, unless my memory fails me, is that you had concluded your examination-in-chief and that we were about to start the cross-examination. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Colonel, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I'm happy to be back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I also wish you a happy new year, and we can now proceed with the various cross-examinations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, are you going first?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No Interpretation] Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kingori.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will start my cross-examination by the very beginning. You carried out some preparations before you arrived in the former Yugoslavia, where you worked as an UN observer. You say that you had a round of preparations first in Kenya, in Nairobi, and then in Zagreb. What I want to know is before you arrived in Srebrenica, did you prepare, did you receive any instructions, any information that pertained to your work in that particular area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the care of preparations that we had before going to Srebrenica was mainly -- mainly a brief on how the situation was, and especially anywhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was always taken to be different from the other areas of the former Yugoslavia, so one had to get a proper brief and proper instructions, proper training on how to handle the situation inside Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it was taken to be more risky as compared to other areas of enclave. Also, the kind of issues inside there were a bit different. By this, I mean you find there was more fighting inside there than other areas like, let's say, Eastern Krajina, where I was for about six months, and also the other areas of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at any rate, you received detailed info on both of the warring parties in and around the Srebrenica enclave; am I right in that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said your principal responsibility was to monitor any violations of the ceasefire agreement. These ceasefire violations, did those include holding or keeping military units inside the enclave, with the obvious exception of Dutch-Bat, who were there as part of the UN contingent?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What there is was that the violations to the ceasefire agreement were several. It's only that I do not have a list on them right now, but they are written. One of them was now that no one should be able to have arms inside a safe area, and that is why all the Muslims were disarmed and all the arms, all the heavy weapons and small arms, machine-guns and all that, were taken to a safe place, and that is the Dutch-Bat compound. That is where they were kept. This was happening in all other demilitarised areas, not just Srebrenica. It's in all other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before your arrival in the enclave during your preparations, were you informed that the Muslim forces in the enclave had been disarmed or had surrendered their weapons to the UN?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was informed about that. And even when I arrived, when I was being shown around, I was taken to Bravo Company compound, where I was shown all the heavy weapons that were taken from the Muslim side. They were there. They were safe under Dutch-Bat protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who were you informed by, I mean, about the fact that the Muslim forces within the enclave had been disarmed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information came from the UN headquarters in Zagreb; the UNMO headquarters also in Zagreb; and, also, when we entered the enclave, from the UNMOs, themselves, who were inside there. The information was available to almost everybody that had to have it. Everybody knew what had been done on the demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, you received instructions back in Zagreb about the way in which you would be sending your reports to your superior command. That was your evidence, wasn't it? Were you told at the time what those reports should comprise?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not get your question. Please say it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any instructions as to what your reports should comprise, the reports that you were -- started admitting to your superior command in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received -- we were told what to put in the report; and, as the military observers, generally there was a lot of -- you know, a lot expected from you, in that you were to report on each and every activity going on inside your AOR; that is, area of responsibility, be it military, humanitarian, or any other type of activities going on around there. One was expected or supposed to report on it to the UN headquarters, because though you may think it may not have a direct impact on the activities going on, that information could be needed by other people in the UN system who could use it for their own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about the information that you forwarded in your reports, did they have the same confidentiality level?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. All the information that we were sending was directly for UN consumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you use codes in order to forward this type of information?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did -- we did not use any codes, because our system was very clear on the line to which you are transmitting that information and to the recipient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You would fax this type of information, would you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were different ways of transmitting this kind of information. One of them was definitely, as you're saying, through a fax. The other one, you could encode and use a radio to transmit, and for the other guys on the other side to decode and get it on paper so that they can understand what you really mean. Also, we could use our own net, our own net; that is, our transmission net, our line. You could talk to somebody and tell him what exactly happening. So there are different means of transmitting, and also maybe a final one, which was a bit difficult, I tell, but still could be done, was to get a copy and take it by road. You can take it as a letter to wherever you want it taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another question: Before you arrived in Srebrenica, did you receive any instructions to take notes?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean, but if it is a matter of taking notes, that was our main occupation. As observers, that was our main occupation, to take notes wherever we went.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That was the responsibility of every single UN observer in the area, was it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It really was. In fact, an independent notebook was our main weapon. That is why we were not harmed. That is all we had, and that is what we were using to write what we found in the field and report the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How many notebooks were you supposed to keep?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no issue of notebooks, the number you're supposed to keep, or the number you're supposed to do anything with. What there was is that you write using whichever means that you can, if it is a notebook, if it is a piece of paper, provided the information reaches whoever needs to have it; that is, the UN system. So there is no limitation of the books you could keep.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If my understanding is correct, you had two notebooks; right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I had two that I used. But notebooks, there was no limitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you use both these notebooks to basically take down the same type of information?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what the reason was for you to actually have two different notebooks, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, one could have even more notebooks. There's no limitation on two. That is first and foremost. Secondly, sometimes you could find you're not seeing the other notebook that you are using, so you pick another new -- new book because they were available. We just go out there, use it, then come back. If later on you still cannot find that one or it's misplaced, you can still take another new, fresh book, and go. If you found the old one, you can still use the old one, to continue it with your notes, because what is important here is not -- we were not doing a bookkeeping. It's not a matter that you've got to continue with the same system. No. It's what you find, what you write, you report. Essentially, that was the main purpose of the notebooks, and that is what we were doing. So it really did not matter how many you had or whether you were to use this notebook for now or for this week or for this month and then the other one for the other month. Really, it did not matter. It's the way you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You recently handed over one of those volumes that you kept to the OTP. I realise that it contains dates up to the 9th of July, to the extent that I've been able to inspect the volume. I didn't have much time. Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You destroyed the other volume. That is what you said. What I'd like to ask is to think back and see if you can remember whether you recorded in that other volume also events leading up to the 9th of July alone.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, in the other notebook, it was information that went all the way up to the last day, almost, I think, the last day of our stay in the enclave. That should have been around 20th, 21st, somewhere there, which I felt if it landed on the Bosnian side, BSA side, I could get myself in trouble. I feared for my life at that time, and some of the issues I had written, I had encoded all the names and other activities that each and every individual had done. I feel -- I felt at that time that if it landed on some people on our way out, anything could have happened to me. So I feared for my own safety, and that is why I destroyed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. You said that, after all; however, what I want to know is this: Speaking of the first volume that you destroyed, did you share the fact with anyone; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That other volume, we were -- the only other person I think we shared with was Major Tetteh, because we were with him there throughout, so at least he knew what was inside there. I may have saved another, you know, something, I can't remember, but to whoever, concerning what was inside there, in that it was a bit sensitive. The activities which were going on there, I had written almost everything. That included the personalities; the activities; you know, the issues they were doing there; you know, everything. It was -- it was very sensitive. It was -- according to me, it was very sensitive and had to be -- had to be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I realise that you and the two remaining UN observers, on the 22nd of July, held a briefing at the UNMO HQ in Zagreb or in Tuzla, I'm not certain based on just this document. What I'd like to ask you is: Do you remember the meeting that the three of you held with the UNMO people? I assume this was some sort of superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at 1D470, which has been marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the title, you see that this was a debrief of UNMOs from the Srebrenica enclave. Do you remember holding a meeting like that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall no longer be requiring this exhibit. We'll be returning to it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But there's another thing I would like to ask you now: Did you receive any instructions, before you arrived in the enclave, about your own freedom of movement? Were you instructed that you were authorised to move throughout the enclave, freely and unhindered?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We got that brief that our freedom of movement was guaranteed, and we could patrol any area within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you encountered no difficulty in that, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did, we did. We encountered several times some restriction of movement from one area to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who caused this trouble for you? Who hampered your movements?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes we could get problems from the BSA side and sometimes from the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that the Republika Srpska Army was there within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. In some areas, they were inside. In some areas, they were deep inside the enclave area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark those areas for us where you encountered the Republika Srpska Army?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where do I mark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's asking you where?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please name the villages and places?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of these areas were to the south, where the BSA were; that is, mainly to the southern -- southern side. That is where we could encounter them and could prevent us from going further into the enclave towards the separation line. They had entered deeper into the enclave, beyond the ceasefire line. So when we tried to go to the ceasefire line, they would prevent us from going there, and that was mainly to the southern side. I can't remember those villages. If you show me a map, I can show you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, exactly. This is what I was going to ask you. If you were shown a map, would that help you remember the names of these villages or at least the specific area to which you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a map available, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I did not expect this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please tell me when it was that this happened, that you encountered RS Army units deep within the enclave, hindering your movements?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember the dates, but definitely they are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You informed your superiors about that, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Having inspected your reports, I encountered no such indications. It would follow, would it not, that this was going on at a time that was not referred to in those reports; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I doubt whether you have all the reports from UNMO Srebrenica to UNMO Tuzla or UNMO Zagreb. I don't think you have all of them. According to what I've gone through, mainly these are reports from -- you know, of our own transmission, but not directly from UNMO Srebrenica to the other consumers. I wish we had daily all of them or daily sit-reps from UNMO Srebrenica. You can find somewhere a certain time or area where we indicated that we were prevented, because I can remember about two or three occasions where we could not be able to penetrate. You could not go beyond a certain point, because the BSA were inside. You could not even go further to see all the area up to the ceasefire line. One of them I remember. I think there's even an indication where our Serb interpreter -- our Muslim interpreter was being asked some questions by the BSA, and they were very much -- very serious on it, and they really did not want to see him there. That is one of the occasions where they were preventing us from going further to the ceasefire line, meaning they were already inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There had been a number of Dutch-Bat officers here to give evidence in this case, people who were holding observation posts in the area at the time, yet none of them ever told us that the BSA ever crossed the confrontation line in order to enter the enclave. You do agree that they would have had to cross the confrontation line in order to access the enclave territory itself, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that that question accurately reflects the evidence that the Chamber has heard to this point. I don't want to make a huge issue out of it, but it's a matter of record. I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it needs to be discussed, it will be discussed in the absence of the witness, that's for sure. I'm not in a position to agree or disagree with you, because I don't want to interfere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not insist on the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed with your next question, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, you said that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, that side occasionally hindered your movement within the enclave. Can you tell us approximately when that was taking place and where?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered that before, but the area, that was mainly to the southern side, the BSA. The BSA were hindering us mainly to the southern side, and this is where they were deep inside, inside the enclave. In fact, most of the time -- some of the times when we were patrolling there, we could find -- we could find them inside and we could talk to them. If you look at the map, you'll find their actual location at that particular moment. They are inside the enclave. You tell them so; they say no. As far as they are concerned, that is their own territory. Also, even the Dutch-Bat, if you remember, it's one of the meetings that we had, and the Dutch-Bat were being told by the Muslims that they have positioned their OP deep, deeper, deeper inside the enclave, allowing the BSA to come closer and deep inside the enclave. That one is there in one of the reports that are already here, so that was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that you did not see the BSA go past these observation posts and the separation lines that were in place?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think one thing to note is that the observation posts -- some of the observation posts were erected deep inside the enclave. The OPs were not all necessarily on the ceasefire line, and this sometimes became the concern of the Muslims, that the Dutch-Bat were erecting their OPs inside the enclave giving the BSA some leeway into coming nearer the OPs, meaning they've already crossed the ceasefire line and into the -- into the Srebrenica safe area; that is, the enclave. So that was there, and it has been documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning your freedom of movement within the enclave, did you have any problems with the Muslim side? Did it happen on occasion that they would hinder your movement or deny access to some parts of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it happened, especially to the -- on the -- this one I can remember, the Bandera Triangle area. In that area, sometimes they were preventing us from going inside there, and we complained. We were complaining, and it's documented also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who it was that hindered your movement, that prevented you from going there? Were those people armed? Were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Bandera Triangle, that was a very active area, so sometimes you find some guys with arms or even some without arms, but they tell you, "No, you cannot go beyond this point." But whether armed or not armed, they tell you that, you think twice before you cross. Of course, you try so you can see the extent which they react, but of course you don't want to go beyond a certain limit. After coming back to Srebrenica, we would report to the Muslims about, you know, that they were denied access to that area, and we would also report it to the UN HQ using the normal channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What explanation were you given, what reason were you given, for the hindering of movement, or rather, denying access to that part of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they were denying us access beyond a certain point, they were just telling us that, "You're not allowed to be over there. We can't let you go beyond there" No reasons were, you know, given at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay within the Srebrenica enclave, you were able to tour a number of villages within the enclave. Did you meet, in any of those, any Muslim armed forces, apart from the area you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'd rarely find any Muslims with arms, very rare, and I think -- I think it's only once or twice that we found, on the streets, you know, Muslims that were armed; but, otherwise, those guys never had arms. I mean, we could not see them armed at all. I think once or twice, but not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever prevented from visiting a facility that you had an interest in, at which weapons or ammunition may be found, or anything else for that matter?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about food warehouses?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because your last -- or your previous question and the answer given could lead to different interpretations. You asked him: "Were you ever prevented from visiting a facility that you had interest in, at which weapons or ammunition may be found, or anything else for that matter?" And the answer was: "No." But I think what needs to be established, first and foremost, is whether he actually ever had the intention or tried to visit or visited any facility, any such facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honours. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then we can understand his answer better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat my question: Did you ever try to enter a facility to try and see whether there were any weapons, or ammunition, or other material which was not allowed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay in Srebrenica, we were not denied -- you know, there was no place where there was arms that we were denied access to or a place we suspected had arms and we wanted to inspect and then were denied, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also visiting all of the observation posts held by Dutch-Bat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. In most cases, we would visit most of them, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you informed about whether the enclave inhabitants were free to leave it? In other words, were they able to leave the enclave without an approval from the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not get what you mean, but the -- we were never told that the Muslims, you know, were free or not free to move. What there is is that there was always no authority given. Because in exiting or entry into Srebrenica, one had to get authority from the BSA. But for the Muslims to leave the enclave, I don't think there was any of that kind of authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you were uncertain whether such an approval was requested or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the kind of entry or exit from the enclave by the Muslims was not in a way that one had the right to get authority, like we were doing, because with us we had the right to request authority to leave or to enter the enclave, and that had to go through all the channels concerned. So that approval can come back as approved or denied. But for the Muslim side, there was no such a system. But what was happening and what we could get was that sometimes they, themselves, were arranging, through their own private ways, on how to get out and how to get in, to get out to get the food supplies or some other supplies through the system that I called earlier the almost mafia system, sort of, in that you pay your way out and then later on you can come back. That system was working, and we reported on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have already testified on that. I'm trying to be precise and put clearer questions to you. Do you know for a fact that the Muslim authorities did not prohibit the enclave inhabitants to leave it? Do you know anything about that; and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to your approval in the enclave, among other things, were you instructed to cooperate with Dutch-Bat that was within the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was normal. I mean, as a UN organ, we were to cooperate in almost everything, one of them being that they were the main suppliers of our food and even water. We were getting most of our supplies through them, the food that we could go there for lunch, that is, hot meals, and then come back. Also earlier on, we were sometimes exchanging information, and also we were holding meetings sometimes together. Observers -- military observers are mainly independent of the other systems, but cooperation, both laterally and also up or down was encouraged, you know. Only that your reporting does not necessarily have to be the same as theirs, because we had our own unique way of reporting, which was different and very, you know, reliable. Since we, as observers, are not armed, we could be able to access any part of the enclave or anywhere else where the Dutch-Bat sometimes could not be able to access. With us, almost every area was open, you know, for us to go. But for any armed troop, be it a Dutch-Bat or any other, there's some areas they could not get access. In fact, some areas they were asking us to escort them to that place so they can see whatever they want.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As a part of that exchange of information with Dutch-Bat, were you also informed of the activities of the Muslim forces that were inside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was no system whereby they should or ought to have reported to us on anything. There was no such a system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, use on your part of the word "activities" is too generic. I would suggest that you specify which activities you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to military activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered that, but you're free to put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As a part of information exchange with Dutch-Bat, were you informed of any military activities of the Muslim side within the enclave and outside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, unless it's on a specific case that maybe you have in point, there was no system whereby they were or ought to have told us about the military activities of, you know, both inside and outside. By this, what I mean is that the -- the way they were reporting, we didn't necessarily have to know what -- what they have seen. But at certain times they could call us. At times they could tell us, if there's anything that they want us to go and investigate, they could ask us to go and investigate a specific case, but not general.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, you used three interpreters during your stay there, two of which were Muslims and one was a Serb. Were they duty-bound to follow your instructions, the instructions issued by the UNMOs, as representatives of the UN?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: They had no independence in their course of action whatsoever, I presume.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I won't insist on it. It is not very significant. I will move on to the events in July 1995. You told us that you were billeted in the PTT building and that you stayed there until the 9th of July, after which you withdrew to the base of the UN at Potocari. First of all, do you recall the size of that building? How many floors does it have?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I can't remember very well, but it was about four or -- I don't -- around four or five. I cannot recall very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were quartered at the top floor, isn't that correct, you and the other UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not. We were at the basement, the bottom, the bottom floor, the bottom one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the building, there was a small military communications room, as you said, in the same building, that is. Can you recall whether there was anything else inside the building, any other offices, institutions, organisations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot remember whether there was anything else, but there was that communication room up there. I think that's -- that's all I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that on the first day of shelling of the enclave, that you told the Srebrenica inhabitants not to leave their houses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We requested them to stay indoors so that they can be slightly safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood your words correctly, at the time Srebrenica town was shelled, I believe you counted some 250 shells which fell on the town that day.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah. We counted around that number -- that number of shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, since the town was shelled so fiercely, why did you not tell the people to leave the town, where they would be safer?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not tell them to do that because, first and foremost, that number of shells were not falling on just one particular place. The 250 are the reported shells, but they were not falling on one particular grid or one particular point. Secondly, where would we have told them to go to? We could not tell them just to leave their places. We could not. In fact, our aim - and that is why later on we tried to establish contact with Peter - was to ensure that in the first place the shelling stopped. That is why we wanted to talk to the BSA side so that they can stop the shelling of that enclave, but not for us to tell the people to leave, because where do we tell them to go. Which area was safe for them? If the enclave, which is a safe area, is not safe for them, now, where else would you have told them to go? So our immediate reaction at that time was to try to tell them to play it safe: "Be safe wherever you are, stay inside. If you go outside, there is a possibility that you will be hit." Even inside the buildings, they weren't safe, but we felt it was slightly safer inside the buildings than out there where you could be hit by shrapnels. So we could not tell them to go to any other place, because even ourselves were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you referred to 250 shells you counted that day, does it mean that they were falling all over the enclave, and that is the number of shells fired at the enclave as a whole and not the town itself?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in our report it's written somewhere that it was Srebrenica and Potocari. I think it is there written somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your assessment, then, it was safer to remain in Srebrenica itself rather than leave the town and go to the nearby forests?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's always good to be safe. That's what I believe. Secondly, a place you know is better than one you really do not know. If you tell them to go into the forests, you don't know who is inside those forests. There could be soldiers, BSA soldiers with small arms, who can actually kill them at once because they can see them. You know, when you're firing with live shells, sometimes you hit, sometimes you miss. So it's a matter of whether you'll be hit or not, and then being not that accurate because you cannot say it is as accurate as small arms, because with small arms you can see your target. With these ones, it is blind. You're estimating that it will land on that particular area. So it was, as far as we were concerned, safer to stay inside than to tell them to go to the bush, because in the bush, you don't know who -- who is inside there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that on that day, surprisingly, and given the intensity of shelling, there weren't too many victims in Srebrenica. You were also surprised to see that the shelling was also aimed at the marketplace, the hospital, and the PTT building, but however that those location were not hit. Are you telling us that the BSA was actually targeting those buildings?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we were concerned, when you see the concentration, that is, the hit the shells are getting around a certain area, obviously you know maybe that is the particular place they are targeting. They may not be getting it directly, but you see that that is their target. That is what they really want to get. That can also be seen from the time - I can't remember whether it was on the 9th or the 8th - when they targeted the PTT building. It is in our report there that we could see they're targeting it. We could see the landing of the shells. You could see the actual targeting of that particular building. It's only they are not getting it. So you can easily get -- from the analysis of the number of incoming shells and the actual places they are landing on, you can easily get that. You can analyse and get where they're targeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I don't know if you intend to belabour this issue further, but he did testify at some length on this issue and how he could actually establish whether a particular site was being targeted or not, when he was being examined in chief. But it's up to you, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thanks. I will just ask a few more questions about this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me this, then: How do you explain that those buildings which were targeted on that day, the marketplace, the hospital, and the PTT building, were not hit? Could it be because the BSA did not have proper weapons to be able to execute that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember saying this earlier, that most of these artillery weapons, most of the times they are inaccurate. They are not very, very accurate. Also, considering that they are high trajectory, that is, it's not a direct hit, and then where you're firing them from is from a blind point; that is, it's not a point where you're seeing your target.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've already explained that. Thank you. I do not wish to waste time on the things you've already mentioned. When one is targeting a target in such an indirect way, could there be an observer placed nearby which reports back on the coordinates so that the targeting can be corrected? I'm not a soldier, myself, but I believe this is how things are usually done when one wants to hit something.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. You're saying it like a soldier, in that most of the time there must be a way of correcting or adjusting. If you don't hit your target, you may try to adjust a bit. That is why you would find, after hitting this place, maybe the next -- the next one from that particular weapon, because it's not all of them. From that particular weapon, you find it may hit maybe slightly to the right. Sometimes they may go even to the center. So all those adjustments, they're done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: However, after missing these three buildings, they didn't engage the same targets the same day in order to finally hit them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're asking -- it's like I was not on their side. I was not there so I don't know what they were actually doing. Only that what I know is they did not hit those targets properly, and especially the hospital. But the marketplace, obviously they hit. They hit the area. They hit the marketplace several times. But the hospital, they were missing it. So I don't know what they were doing on their side, but mine was just an assessment that maybe that's what they were targeting. It's just that they were not -- they were not hitting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I want to move on to the 8th of July, the second day of shelling, when you were informed by the Chief of Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that over 100 shells had landed on Srebrenica. Tell me this, please: Were you in Srebrenica at all on the 8th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, please, to find what I'm looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was able to locate a statement given by your interpreter, Hasan Mahanovic [as interpreted], provided on the 22nd of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 1D451. Hasan Nuhanovic. Can we please move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 2, it says that because of the shelling just before the fall of Srebrenica, the UNMOs, on the 8th of July, abandoned their positions. Is that true, sir, and that he was the only one who remained there to send information on what was going on?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not correct. Hasan Nuhanovic was never left in our PTT building when we left. When we abandoned the PTT building, we did not leave him there. In the first place, he was not there,, he was out in the field, as far as we were concerned. We tried to look for him. We waited for him. We could not get him, and he was somewhere out there, looking for his relatives. We have written our report on that. It is somewhere in what you already have, but he was away and that is why we only left with the other interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you can't rule out the possibility that you left Srebrenica on the 8th of July, as he says, can you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we need to get to where we left. I think there's a report on when we left the enclave -- the PTT building. It is somewhere here. So if you can get it, I can get the actual date. But the point is we did not leave Hasan Nuhanovic in our PTT building. In fact, when we were leaving, when we left in the evening, he was not there. We could not find him. It was we left around 6.00 and we dismantled everything, including our communication. So we could not have left him to continue communicating to anybody. There was nothing left in that PTT building, as far as UNMO activities were concerned. There was nothing at all for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you were not in touch with him again before the fall of Srebrenica, were you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasan, we were not in touch with --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: With Hasan Nuhanovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasan Nuhanovic, we were not in touch with him until much, much letter, when he appeared in the Dutch-Bat compound. He's the one who brought himself to the Dutch-Bat compound much later, and he said he was out there looking for his relatives, who he did not know where they were and he had to stay there looking for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to our information, on the 9th [as interpreted] Of July a member of Dutch-Bat named "Renssen" was killed. Did you go there to see exactly what happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment before you answer the question. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this objection may need to be heard outside the presence of the witness, and it is one -- it is one that I absolutely need to make on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine. Could you please accompany the witness outside the courtroom. Colonel, I'm sure you understand we need to discuss a procedural matter which cannot be discussed in your presence or which shouldn't be discussed in your presence. We'll soon call you -- we'll soon call you back, unless we take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think it's been virtually uncontested, and this may be just a slip of the mind, but the evidence has been clear and, I think, virtually uncontested that Private van Renssen died on the 8th of July and not on the 9th of July. I think the evidence has been ample; and as my friend is obviously making an issue of dates, I wanted to state that objection but outside the presence of the witness. If my friend does have evidence that he suggests establishes that that death occurred on the 9th. I am more than happy to hear that, but I just wanted to clarify that before things got confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was my mistake. Sorry. Yes, it was on the 8th of July. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we take the break now or bring in the Colonel again? For the record, while we were sitting, we were informed that Mr. Borovcanin was on his way to the Tribunal; in fact, he is present now. Shall we have the break or what do you suggest? We will have the break now. Please explain to the witness that we are having a break, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've been told, Mr. Haynes, you wish to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That may be putting it a little strongly, but I -- I was true to my undertaking to talk with Mr. McCloskey during the course of the last break about the 65 ter motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think I can say, without fear of contradiction, we're confident we can work towards a position where we won't need to trouble you with a decision on that motion. We're going to, as it were, crystallise any potential areas of dispute over which particular documents traverse; and without disassembling, I think the position is that where there is agreement, Mr. McCloskey will simply not use those documents in direct examination of Mr. Butler. I think I speak collectively when I say that, given that that is an issue, it will likely take us until Monday morning to resolve; and given the state of preparation of Mr. Butler for his evidence and the significance of him as a witness in this case, I think wherever we get to with Mr. Kingori, during the course of today and tomorrow, we would collectively appreciate Mr. Butler making a clean start on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I, frankly, think that is more likely to be the case, in any case, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President and everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On the last point, I actually brought that up as well to Mr. Haynes and all Defence counsel on being able to organise Mr. Butler to start Monday, given the estimates for Kingori. That would be of great assistance in organising, continuing to organise, finishing the organisation of the many documents, because of e-court and we're finding the usual issues. But I think in the end it would save time for me to be able to schedule Mr. Butler for Monday so that I would be able to schedule speaking to him and organising these voluminous documents. So that's something I join and actually helped initiate with Defence counsel. And on the 65 ter issues, where I agree, I won't use a document. Where we disagree, if that occurs, we'll -- we'll be able to isolate to you where we disagree, so that you can decide the issue rather quickly tomorrow or Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Anything else? All right. Let's bring in the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, it's up to you to decide whether you want to repeat your last questions using the correct date or whether you want to abandon it and move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll correct my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, I will repeat the question that I asked you before the break. I made a small error concerning the date. According to our information, on the 8th of July, 1995, Dutch-Bat Private van Renssen was killed. My question is: Did you go to the scene and did you ascertain the circumstances under which he had been killed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this private was, as far as I can remember, killed by -- by an impact, I think, from the BSA side. I'm not very sure about it. But maybe if you can show me the record, maybe I can remember. I cannot remember that one. But I know he was killed and I know about the report, and I think I was involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Did you personally go there to ascertain the circumstances and cause of his death?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not personally do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this something that was done by your other colleagues, another military observer, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, another military observer. I cannot remember who that was. But anything done by a military observer, we own it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you tell anyone about the cause of Private Renssen's death?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Anyone." I don't understand what you mean by "anyone," but we reported about it. We reported.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, again, I mean, the question that you put to him is a little bit tricky, at least as the way we have had it translated. You asked him specifically about reporting about the cause of Private Renssen's death, not the death itself but the cause. I don't think that, from his previous answer, he gave an indication that he was aware of the cause of Private Renssen's death. So I think you have to either rephrase your question or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'll -- I'll leave this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that one of the things discussed at your meetings with BH representatives in the enclave was also the attacks and ambushes set up by the BS Army against the Muslims who were on their way back from Tuzla, where they had travelled to, to collect certain goods and supplies. You do remember that, sir, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us exactly what sort of goods or supplies they were bringing back from Tuzla? I'll try to be more specific. Did that include weapons, ammunition, and the like?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, not as far as I am aware of. In other words, what I know is that the kind of goods they were bringing back were food stuffs and that kind of thing, but of course we never went anywhere to inspect what they were bringing back. But I'm aware mainly, you know, most of the goods they were bringing in was food stuffs for the locals, because there was no food inside the enclave other than what the UNHCR was giving them. So mainly those are the supplies they were bringing in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you never went to inspect or carried any inspections, how come you know exactly what they were bringing in? What's the source of your information, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the source of information was the resupply in the local market. Whenever these guys went out, you could see the amount of goods that had been brought in are more than you had seen maybe the previous day, the previous week, or something like that, because we were monitoring the prices of goods and you could find now the goods are more than they were before, meaning there has been a resupply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But if there were no inspections, this fact alone does not rule out the possibility that weapons were also being brought over from Tuzla; is that correct? You wouldn't expect, if weapons were also being transported from Tuzla, you wouldn't find those in the market?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely, if -- if the arms were being brought in, you wouldn't expect them to be in the market. But at least you could know or you could hear, because we were talking with these people almost continuously. Sometimes, yes, they may not reveal that they have brought in weapons. But as far as we knew, there were no weapons, you know, coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, I understand you're claiming that no weapons or ammunition were being sold openly; therefore, it is your inference that those people who went to Tuzla never brought back any weapons or ammunition. Is that your inference, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is correct. That is what I'm talking about. But also, on the other hand, since the agreement for these people to get out was -- and come in was being done by the BSA through, you know, using their local contacts and the payments therein, I don't expect these people could have allowed the Muslims also to bring in weapons to fight them. So it's our conviction that definitely they were just bringing in food stuffs and other essential commodities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have Exhibit 1D464. It seems that it has not yet been translated, although we put in a request for this last month. I will tell you what sort of a document this is. This is a letter to the -- by the General Staff of the BH Army to the 1st Corps Command. This is an interim report by Army General Rasim Delic. The report was submitted on the 13th of July, 1995. It talks about the aid that was delivered into the enclave by the BH Army, 2nd Corps. Can we please move on to the next page of this document. There is a table there indicating the items that were delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At number 1, we see "Bullet," "7.62 times 39." That's what it says. Then under "Srebrenica," it says "354.656 items" or "pieces." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 658, yes, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Then you see other types of bullets being mentioned: 7.62 times 54, 20.000 of those; 7.9-millimetre, 26.520; and then rifle launch grenade, 35 of those; 96 hand grenades, 425; RPG with the optical site, probably, 44; and then RPG, 7; missiles, 292; hand-held grenades, 59; and then a rocket-launcher, 107-millimetre, one; and then 107-millimetre missiles, 28 of those. There are a lot of items in this table. I'm not going to take you through the entire list. But my question is: Is it possible for all of these to be brought into the Srebrenica enclave without the UN observers noticing anything?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I can tell you is that these kind of weapons, there seems so many that have come in without us knowing, although of course we were not patrolling each and every corner daily, each and every minute, each and every hour. But at the same time these kind of weapons, for them to have come in at least to Srebrenica, I think is a little bit difficult for us to contemplate. I doubt, I doubt, unless they were kept somewhere near the forest or somewhere that we could not tell. Because most of the activities going on inside there, we had to have a bit of knowledge about it. These kind of weapons, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, you said that one of the things discussed at your meetings with the BH authorities in the enclave was also the frequent objections following attacks on villages, especially those in the Bandera Triangle. That was part of your evidence here. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you also said that ordinary farmers were often attacked on those occasions. How did you know that the people who came under attack on those occasions were just ordinary farmers?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we could go there to investigate, and the people we were talking to, we -- we found they were just ordinary farmers, and that is -- that is the evidence we used. You know, they are there, you can see they are normal farmers, and that's it. They were not armed, they were not in combat -- combat gear and all that; and so their activities, at least you could see, they are farming. They have farms, so that's why we could ordinarily report that they were farmers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understood you to be saying that you had no access to the Bandera Triangle. Sometimes you were stopped by armed people and sometimes you were stopped by unarmed people. That was in answer to one of my previous questions during this examination.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm under the impression that this is not consistent with what you're telling us now; namely, that when looking at those people who were inside the Bandera Triangle, you concluded that those were ordinary farmers, unarmed, those who were subjected to attacks. Do you not find a contradiction there, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no contradiction. What there is -- what there is is that when the attack occurred or when an attack occurred and we went there to investigate, the injured and those whose farms the bombs had fallen on, you find they're ordinary farmers. That does not mean that we were not stopped earlier or would not be stopped later by people who were armed. It does not change any of those, because the stopping could not -- is not necessarily in the same place. The Bandera Triangle was big. And when you find ordinary farmers farming in their fields, and they had, that does not mean that you would not be stopped the following day by an armed soldier. So it's a bit different and it's not necessarily a contradiction. It's only that the people we found there during those attacks were ordinary farmers, but at the same time we have also reported that at times we were stopped by armed people. That does not contradict each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You knew that they were ordinary farmers because, when you spoke to them, they carried no weapons, and they said so; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, not that alone. I've just said that, first and foremost, they said they were ordinary farmers. Secondly, you would find them carrying out the farming activities. You would find them there, in the farms, carrying out their ordinary farming activities, and that would force you to believe that they are actually ordinary farmers. Also, another factor is sometimes you find their ages, some of them were old, old men and women, who ordinarily would not be at war, would not be armed, I mean, would not be soldiers. So you're forced to believe that actually these -- these are ordinary farmers. If you found a young, energetic, and highly versatile people, then you may think that these can easily convert to soldiers at night or during other times. But when you find some of these old people, you know, they are just in their farms, they have their implements and all that, you believe these are farmers, and that is what convinced us that that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying there were no military targets in the Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that. What I meant is in that area -- part of that area, we were not allowed to go. So, I mean, the areas we were allowed to go, we could see there were no military targets. But maybe in the areas we were not accessing, maybe they were, maybe they were not. But as far as we were concerned, the areas we were going, we were finding farmers going on with their normal farming activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You also say that, in a way, you were taken aback to hear that members of the Republika Srpska Army had requested that the Muslims leave the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean, but of course at one point or other the BSA had told us that they -- they didn't want the Muslims inside the enclave. It is on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And they stated no reason for that, did they?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They gave varying reasons or many reasons that they were giving. One of them, and it's on record here, is that they did not want to have Muslims who were supported by fundamentalists in their midst. They did not want to have a country where they have Muslims supported by fundamentalists. Another point was that they really felt uncomfortable with Muslims living inside their own area, because they believed that area belonged to the -- to the Serbs. So they didn't want them there. There are varying reasons, and it's all documented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Zivanovic, if I can interrupt a minute. I thought you would ask some more questions on the death of Private Renssen. Mr. Kingori, you answered to Mr. Zivanovic that, as far as you can remember, Private Renssen was killed by an impact from the BSA. Could you expand on that? Could you tell us, as far as you can remember, how he died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for taking me back slightly. With this soldier, I also remember saying that I am not the one who went to investigate; though, as observers, we owned up to that report. We are the ones who made that report, and I cannot remember fully. He was killed by a shell. Actually, I think it was either a bullet or something, but I cannot remember very well from which side it came from. But I think it was from the BSA, only that I'm not very sure about it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your base why you think it was from the BSA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because it was in an OP -- or maybe I'm confusing the two incidents altogether, because I can remember very well there was one who was killed by the BSA and there was another who was killed by the Muslims when they were trying to withdraw. So in these two scenarios, I cannot remember which one exactly is which one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on your last answer, I realise that two Dutch-Bat members were killed on that occasion. Is my understanding correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, there are two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know who the other soldier was, what his name was, since we have never heard of the other one, really?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, I don't have the names of either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned the fact that the Republika Srpska Army units took up the Echo or Eco Observation Post?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to that, had there been any warnings or explanations as to why this would be done?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, the taking of the OPs by the Bosnian Serbs was not in a system that maybe there were discussions that, "We are going to take it, or it will not be taken," only that they would launch an attack and take the OP. To them, they felt that, as far as they were concerned, there were some Muslim soldiers around the OPs, and that is what they wanted to finish. And at the same time, when they were -- they were attacking the OPs, to them it was an advancement. They were going more towards the enclave, and also prevent them being observed from those OPs. So it was multi-pronged, in that it was multifaceted. They were looking at different things so that they can reach their objective and be closer, and also not be observed in their activities by the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, were you ever there for any meetings related to this observation post, the Echo Observation Post? Were you in touch with representatives of the Republika Srpska Army when this was discussed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which meeting was that, if I may, because I'm not very sure which meeting that was? But on OP Echo alone, maybe I need to refer to the document, because I cannot remember whether that -- or concerning that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any explanations or announcements from any Dutch-Bat members, for example, that the Republika Srpska Army was about or had every intention to take OP Echo?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had that. The -- either the CO Dutch-Bat or his deputy or the LO team once mentioned to us that the BSA are intending to taking over the -- in fact, it's not taking over. Those guys had said that the OP be removed from its -- from that particular location. That is what they had told the Dutch-Bat, to remove the OP. Then if later on when it was not removed when Dutch-Bat said or insisted that they cannot remove the OP, I think that is when they -- they went in there and took over the OP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will show you a statement given by one of the officers of Dutch-Bat. His name was Evert Rave, and he was under commands, direct subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number of the statement is 1D452. Let us go to page 3 of the statement, please, the penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read it to yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The penultimate one: [In English] "The 31st May meeting was held at Observation Post Echo. The Serbian representatives were ..." Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you notified of this conversation between Dutch-Bat representatives with the representatives of the BSA concerning these activities on the Muslim side that they complained about?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing we got from these people was that the BSA were complaining that the OP should be removed, as it was being used by the Muslims. Nothing more than that. And further to that, these reports by -- by Dutch-Bat were not necessarily all of them communicated to us. So most of the things we would not get, so -- but at least we got that concerning the reason why the BSA wanted the OP removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it true that Muslims made use of UN observation posts?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the OPs were Dutch-Bat. We had no OPs of our own. So if they were used by -- if they were being used by the Muslims, really we were not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among others, we heard statements here and testimonies of some Dutch-Bat officers. I can tell you that one of them told us - and he was a deputy commander of the battalion by the name of "Franken" - among other things he said that upon his arrival to Srebrenica, he was told that the Muslim forces within the enclave had between four and four and a half thousand pieces of light weapons and a number of mortars. In the transcript, it is page 2438, lines 11 to line 2 on the next page. Were you told perhaps that the Muslim forces in the enclave, at the time of your arrival, were in possession of some four to four and a half thousand pieces of infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when you say "infantry weapons," I hope you mean light weapons, small arms. As far as we were concerned, all the heavy weapons and the machine-guns were all in the custody of Dutch-Bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've told us that. I'm asking about light weapons now.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Light weapons in the possession of the -- of the Muslims, we ourselves, let's say myself, I was not aware that officially they had those weapons. I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
